title: Far-right media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos deported by ICE from US to UK | US immigration - The Guardian
raw_text: Far-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US after being detained on Thursday by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in New Orleans in connection with what the agency said was expired authorization to be in the country and a deportation order. Yiannopoulos’s deportation to the UK occurred on Friday, said a statement on Saturday from a spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE. A DHS spokesperson on Friday said that Yiannopoulos, 41, had been arrested by ICE on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans international airport. The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019 through New York City but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”. The spokesperson said that Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”. The spokesperson added: “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.” Yiannopoulos – who has previously been a vocal supporter of ICE and immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residency – was believed to have been arrested while heading to a concert by rapper Ye, formerly Kanye West. West performed at New Orleans’s Caesars Superdome on Friday. In 2022, Yiannopoulos worked on West’s short-lived 2024 White House campaign, and his social media account suggests he was working for a company of the rapper. Yiannopoulos, a former editor of the conservative media outlet Breitbart News, previously served as an intern for the former US congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene. He eventually became locked into a feud with fellow far-right commentator Laura Loomer, a Trump administration ally who claimed on Friday that she had reported Yiannopoulos to ICE over his immigration status. At the peak of his influence, Yiannopoulos was offered a speaking slot at the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, in 2017 after he had been supportive of Donald Trump during his run for his first presidency. He fell out of favor in conservative circles after the publication of a video in which he condoned sexual relations with boys as young as 13. Yiannopoulos claimed that his experiences as a victim of teenage sexual abuse gave him license to comment on the subject. He soon resigned as a senior editor at Breitbart. Yiannopoulos was also banned from Twitter, now called X, in 2016 for directing racist and misogynistic tweets against a Black actor in a Ghostbusters remake. His account was reinstated to the platform in 2022 after it was acquired and renamed by multibillionaire Elon Musk. A little more than a year before his detention by ICE, a social media post from Yiannopoulos called on immigration checkpoints to be set up at California “supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersection and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally”. He had also sarcastically asked whether it was impolite for one “to masturbate” in public rather than in private “if you are going about your business and find yourself observing an ICE raid” amid the mass deportation campaign that Trump has pursued throughout his second presidency.

title: Licence loss, fines for companies hosting migrants in shoddy housing - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: The Victorian Labour Hire Authority has tightened regulation of businesses that provide accommodation for their workers. Labour hire providers that do not comply with standards could lose their licence and face fines of more than $160,000. What's next? Migrant advocacy groups hope the rules can be applied in other states and territories. Labour hire companies that house migrant workers in substandard accommodation will risk losing their licence as part of a new crackdown. The Victorian Labour Hire Authority has launched new licence conditions after a series of cases in which migrant workers were housed in poor conditions. The authority, which works to prevent the exploitation of labour hire workers, brought in the conditions for businesses that provide housing for their workers. The conditions have been put in place for providers in industries such as horticulture and meat processing, which have high rates of worker exploitation. In addition to losing their licences, businesses that do not comply face fines of more than $160,000. The authority's director of intelligence, compliance and enforcement Erin Barlow said the changes were aimed at protecting vulnerable workers. "We know that when accommodation is tied to employment, workers can feel unable to complain because they can be fearful of losing both their job and their housing," she said. "These workers are especially vulnerable to exploitation." Ms Barlow said the new conditions were in response to substandard worker accommodation the authority had seen. In December 2025, the authority found 22 migrant workers were housed in unsanitary conditions in a single home and a granny flat in Gippsland. The accommodation in Warragul, about an hour east of Melbourne, had sewage pooling in the front yard and black mould covering doors, windows, ceilings and curtains. "In that case, we saw some of the worst accommodation that we had experienced," Ms Barlow said. "Providers can expect to see us out and about inspecting that accommodation more now that we are introducing these conditions. "Accommodation is a clear focus for the Labour Hire Authority in the next year." 'Not fit for an animal' Migrant Justice Institute co-executive director Bassina Farbenblum has welcomed the change. "We've seen for a long time that migrant workers are subjected to really appalling accommodation," she said. "It's terrific to see that the Victorian Labour Hire Authority is now ramping up. "The proof will be how well it is enforced. Hopefully we will see really strict enforcement." Ms Farbenblum said living in unhygienic and overcrowded accommodation was "incredibly demeaning". "We've heard from many migrant workers … the ability to sleep and function is diminished, there's issues with privacy and especially for women there are real safety issues. "I had one migrant worker describe [their accommodation] as 'not fit for an animal'," she said. "I'd hope that other states like New South Wales will follow and that we will start to see a real shift in the impunity of labour higher providers that don't provide habitable, decent accommodation to vulnerable migrants." Industry backs new conditions Victorian Farmers Federation horticulture president Michael Crisera said the change was a good step for the industry. "We're definitely supportive of improving conditions for our workers," he said. "Any industries with labour hire involved definitely need some more compliance." Mr Crisera said there needed to be education for labour hire providers about what the standards were, as well as education for workers. "Everybody needs to play a part in making sure that it's a win-win for the staff and also for the farmer," he said. Accommodation standards already existed but sat with other bodies, such as local councils and Consumer Affairs Victoria. The standards are now a part of some labour hire licence conditions, which allows the Labour Hire Authority to take action against businesses that do not comply. The conditions are being applied to new labour hire licences in the horticulture, meat and poultry processing, commercial cleaning, and security industries and will be rolled out to existing licence holders in those sectors in coming months.

title: Inside Papua New Guinea's secret political refugee crisis - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: Each election cycle in PNG sparks conflicts and tribal violence leading to mass displacement of thousands of people around Papua New Guinea, but especially in the highlands. You'll hear from a journalist who borne witness to this violence, a human rights advocate walking alongside the refugees, and a police commissioner trying to negotiate peace. Talent: Rebecca Kuku, PNG Journalist Ruth Kissam, President Advancing PNG Women Leaders Joseph Tondop, Acting Assistant Police Commissioner Highlands Western End Presenter: Scott Waide This edition of Politok was a repeat of the program broadcast on the 6th of May 2025 Credits Image Details Scott Waide: Election time in Papua New Guinea is tense and chaotic. News clip: Escalating violence has engulfed the Papua New Guinea elections with reports of up to 18 people being killed in the Enga Highlands. Scott Waide: Millions of people in more than 20 provinces turn out to vote, but it's not always free and not always fair. Rebecca Kuku: We literally saw kids voting and there was no privacy, like you couldn't just cast your vote. All the scrutineers of candidates that were contesting would stand at the ballot, where the ballot box was and where you were supposed to vote. And they would all see you put that mark. Scott Waide: In 2022, journalist Rebecca Kuku was in the highlands of Papua New Guinea, in Enga and Hela provinces, reporting as voting chaos turned to terror. Rebecca Kuku: So it was very scary. There was no law. There was no respect for law. They didn't follow the election laws. Scott Waide: In the highlands, tribal rivalries have people on edge and ownership of illegal guns is on the rise. And when election comes around, this can mix quickly and turn deadly. Rebecca Kuku: During the election, one tribe supported one candidate and the other tribe supported the other candidate. All the supporters of the candidates were there, fully armed, you know, sweaty. You could just feel the tension in the air. Scott Waide: Hi, I'm Scott Waide and this is Politok, a show taking you behind the scenes of Pacific politics and how it affects us. Over the coming episodes, I'll be speaking with politicians from across the Pacific region and with everyday people about the political experiences that shape us. I'll uncover the stories and unpack the big questions. Today on PoliTalk, every election cycle in Papua New Guinea, thousands of people are displaced and many are killed. And I want to know why this keeps happening and why isn't anyone talking about it? And a warning, this episode contains mention of sexual violence. Rebecca Kuku has seen it all. She's an experienced journalist in Papua New Guinea and she's reported on everything from dodgy politicians to sorcery accusations. But even still, in 2022, while reporting on that year's election, she was shocked at what she saw. Rebecca Kuku: So the 2022 elections was crazy. We literally saw kids voting. There was no privacy, like you couldn't just cast your vote. All the scrutineers of candidates that were contesting would stand at the ballot, where the ballot box was and where you were supposed to vote. And they would all see you put that mark so they can record it on their books. Scott Waide: Across many parts of the country, chaos reigned. There were delays to polling schedules, ballot boxes weren't arriving on time, and there were allegations of vote buying. The mistrust in the process, coupled with underlying tribal tensions, saw buildings burn to the ground and women and children massacred. Rebecca Kuku: It was really frustrating to see all the stuff that happens during the elections. We just had to stand there and watch them do whatever they wanted to do. Scott Waide: Rebecca, violence during election time is common because there's a level of distrust in the government and the election process. But you were in the highlands where there's also a big link between tribal violence that bleeds into election time. How does that link work? Rebecca Kuku: So, for example, let's talk about Poguera. So in Poguera, there's an existing tribal fight there. Between about 20 to 25 clans break it down into four tribes or three tribes, and they have this land dispute tribal fight that was already there. So when the election came about, it just, it just added up again. During the election, one tribe supported one candidate and the other tribe supported the other candidate. And then it just led into an all-out war again, tribal war. So there were about, I think, over 20 clans clashed. And people were displaced and a lot of families, especially the public servants that were serving in Poguera, like doctors and service teachers, they had to get their families and they had to get out of there. They had to travel in the night back to Hagan to find refuge. And those that couldn't afford to travel or didn't have any relatives in Hagan that they could stay with just went into the bushes and they were living in the bushes. Scott Waide: What triggers the violent outbreaks during elections? Rebecca Kuku: Most of the fights broke up during the ballot box picking. There was tension, there were arguments, there were a few fistfights and all that during the campaign period and during when the ballot box was inserted into the voting areas. But the fights broke up when officials went in to pick up the ballot boxes. In some cases they bent ballot boxes and in other cases they didn't want people to vote and they just hijacked ballot boxes. Scott Waide: In the 2022 election, the United Nations estimated that 90,000 people were displaced because of the violence that broke out. When people in the highlands had to flee, what did that look like? Rebecca Kuku: The mothers and the children, especially the old, they would go up into the mountains and they'd hide in the bushes. There was no way for them, they couldn't seek refuge anywhere. So the only thing they did at the time was to hide in the bushes. And those who had intermarriages close by villages in Anga, they went there to seek refuge. But even so, when they went to seek refuge in the nearby villages, it was very difficult for them. When you go into someone else's territory, they got bullied again. So it was very hard, especially for the girls. There were so many girls that were sexually abused, assaulted and there was nothing done about it. There was no justice sought for them. Scott Waide: The violence and the displacement comes during election time can have a huge impact on children in particular. Is there a story about how it's affected children that stuck with you? Rebecca Kuku: So one of those stories that I heard that really left an impression on me was how a young boy tried to save his mom. So the father was a supporter of a candidate. He was very vocal in supporting him. So the other candidates, supporters, they went to their house and they burned down their house. They pulled women and girls and this little six-year-old boy took his mom and they went up into the bushes and he hid his mom up in the bushes. That was very tough to see that a child so used to the violence knew what to do and how to protect his mother because the father wasn't there. There have also been stories of school children that were raped during the election violence, especially girls in high school, secondary schools, who were just caught up in between them. I mean, from going to school and coming back, some of them were caught up in the election violence and they were sexually assaulted, but nothing was ever done about it because it was just chaos out there and police had their hands full. All these young girls, they were just assaulted. Scott Waide: In the media, there are lots of headlines and reporting about tribal violence, but there isn't a lot of coverage of election violence and the displacement that comes with it. Why is that? Rebecca Kuku: Well, it's very sad because most of the stories don't get published. It doesn't get the coverage it needs to be in order to raise that issue. In PNG, because of the most of these people that were displaced, they just go on to live with relatives or go on to live with their in-laws from the nearby villages. And despite the challenges they face there, they have nowhere else to go. So they just stay and make a new place their home. It's been very tough trying to get those stories out. Scott Waide: The picture Rebecca paints is of a crisis that's being swept under the rug. Tens of thousands of people, families, women and children must flee their homes, their customary land, every time there's an election because of tribal tensions and a distrust of the electoral system. There's also the growing threat of illegal firearms, adding fuel to a raging fire. And for decades, Ruth Kisam has been trying to put that fire out. Ruth Kissam: I'm Ruth Kisam. I call myself a community organizer, human rights activist, but I am currently the president of the Advancing PNG Women Leaders Network, an amazing network of community-based organization across 15 provinces. Scott Waide: Ruth is a peace-building activist, and over the course of her career, she's stood by the side of women and families in the region, advocating for an end to violence. Ruth Kissam: You don't set out to be a peace-builder, but your work actually draws you into it. Scott Waide: Ruth is from the Highlands in Enga province. She's also well-known for her work around sorcery accusation-related violence, which began after a chance encounter at a hospital. Ruth Kissam: I ended up at the hospital, taking my dad to the hospital, and then I saw this notice that was put up on the notice board, followed the prompt on the notice board to claim a body that was unclaimed for some time, and then claiming the body and burying her, later finding out that she was killed on accusations of sorcery. Fast forward three years later, I found out that she had a daughter, and the daughter was also tortured on accusations of sorcery. So that also now sort of dragged me into it after the rescue, and I basically took my work home, and my work is my daughter. So I have a vested interest now, it's a personal one, to be in this space and to do what I do. Scott Waide: Ruth, you witnessed firsthand the election violence that happened in 2022. What was it like for you? Ruth Kissam: It was one of the worst elections that I've ever witnessed, and it caused a lot of displacement when people started turning violent. All villages, all tribes were wiped off their land. Even to this day, there's people that have not even gone back to their homes, and they're living in other provinces. They've set up camps in other provinces. What land in other provinces? Mosby has some of those, Leah has some of those, Hagen has most of those. So people are living internally in Papua New Guinea as refugees within the country. Scott Waide: Can you explain how tribal allegiances influences elections? Ruth Kissam: The interesting thing about politics in Papua New Guinea is no one is interested in policies, because it becomes a tribal matter. So people will affiliate with you because of their tribal affiliation, or in other parts, yes, it's your policy, but it's also your party affiliation. So it's more along the lines of who I know than what I want to know about that person. If I know that person, if I know someone that knows him, then I will align with him. And from my experience, especially up in the highlands where I'm from, it's always to do with how your tribe is linked to this person or your family. Unfortunately, in these circumstances, a lot of people that are running for elections usually go by their rest houses or where the polling booths are. So if this person has about two or three polling booths in his tribal land, now they don't care about the ward or the LLGs. For them, it's how they're affiliated to a tribe, whether it's from their mother's side or their father's side. And if that's the case, then the ballot boxes are there. So then it usually ends up being a tribal block vote. Scott Waide: And how did you see this play out in the 2022 elections? Ruth Kissam: One classic example is one up in the recent 2022 elections up in the Ambon-Kompiem district where it pretty much affected the whole of Enger province was what they call the seven in one. So seven tribes actually ganged up against one tribe because of displacement happening well over 8,000, 9,000 people simply because of tribal affiliation. So the displacement is coming about because of tribal affiliation. Those elections are now proving to be the triggers. So once the elections are coming about, sometimes it resurfaces old tribal wars. Scott Waide: Although the 2022 election was bad, election violence happens every time people go out to vote. How have you seen this kind of violence impact people over the years? Ruth Kissam: So one of the stories of a family member, a family that I married into. So back in 2012, a house was burned, election related. She rebuilt it. 2017, the house got burned. She rebuilt it. 2022, the house got burnt again. All of the times the house got burnt was not a tribal fight. It was election related. So this is a woman that was highly traumatized. But in 2022, she had her granddaughters with her, two granddaughters. I think one was five and I think the other one was three or something. They actually ended up at a creek and not only herself, but she and other women as well. And this creek actually housed them for two or three nights, three days. They couldn't even get out. They couldn't move around because people were rampaging through their village, burning down, killing, mutilating people and raping women and children. So for them was that they just, and they survived by the creek, you know, drinking from the water, just not going anywhere because that was the only place that they could find refuge. And then they walked for another day or so just to reach safety. Now, this is just one and this is a woman in her late 50s, early 60s. And that's just one. You can imagine what's happening with others, women and children. For some, the mother said she couldn't find her daughter, later found out that the daughter drowned while trying to cross the big river. And she wasn't the only one. Others also. Scott Waide: Thousands of people flee this violence each time there's an election and these political refugees are moving to other provinces, other tribal lands. What's the experience like for them? Ruth Kissam: So, you know, the thing about internally displacement of people is culture plays also a very critical role. In a culture like Gela, they'll never even get a branch from another tribal land without permission for firewood. So when people are internally displaced and given refuge by another tribe, they can only get what is allowed to them. They will not get anything that is not allowed to them. So when they don't have food, when they don't have water and all of that, it makes it really hard. So now they will have to look for something better for themselves. title: Britain knew about the Holocaust as it happened. A new exhibition reckons with that truth - The Guardian
raw_text: The “complex and unsettling” story of what Britain knew during the Holocaust is being explored amid plans to create a new permanent national memorial. An exhibition highlighting how news of the atrocity reached Britain much earlier than is commonly understood will tour the country after being viewed privately by MPs at Portcullis House on the parliamentary estate at Westminster in September. The research draws upon newspaper reporting, broadcasts, academic scholarship, witness testimony and government archives. The exhibition is a sample of a more extensive, permanent exhibition for the national Holocaust Memorial and Learning Centre, which is planned for a site in London. Martin Winstone, the senior historical adviser to the Holocaust Educational Trust, said: “There’s a feeling today that Britain really only found out about the Holocaust at the end of the war. But in 1942, the year in which most victims of the Holocaust were murdered, you couldn’t really escape this information in Britain. It was in every newspaper. It was on the BBC. “The Manchester Guardian was the newspaper that reported most extensively on the Holocaust, taking a crusading position that there was more the British government and allied governments could be doing.” For years, the Manchester Guardian, which was banned from Germany in 1933 for highlighting Adolf Hitler’s antisemitism, called for immigration restrictions to be lifted for Jews, lobbied for pressure to be applied to neutral nations to open their borders to refugees and for special rescue measures, realising that “the Nazis were aiming at the complete elimination of an entire group of people”. Much of the information about the Holocaust, including the locations of death camps, was smuggled out of Poland – where the murders were “happening in plain sight” – by couriers to the London-based Polish government-in-exile. Winstone said: “It was a challenging situation. There were lots of things the government had to deal with. And for much of that war, Britain was on the defensive. “On one level, the government’s response was always, ‘we’ll win the war, that’s how we stop this’; while critics said, ‘there’ll be nobody left to save, if that’s what you’re waiting for’.” During the second world war, the government commissioned reports on antisemitism in Britain, with agents opening people’s mail and recording conversations overheard in air raid shelters to gauge public opinion. In what Winstone described as a “complex and unsettling story”, Ministry of Information bulletins revealed that while there was mass public sympathy for Jews in occupied Europe, it contended with anti-migration and antisemitic sentiment. Winstone added: “Nearly everybody in Britain was disgusted about these mass murders, but at the same time you start getting more antisemitic discourse about Jews in Britain – that Jews were running the black market, avoiding military service and spreading panic. “Even before the mass murder began, during the 1930s, there was a significant body of opinion which felt Britain should not be admitting refugees.” Winstone said UK immigration laws in the 1930s were highly restrictive, in part because of antisemitism earlier in the 20th century. But after the Kristallnacht pogrom of 1938, Britain relaxed restrictions to some extent, allowing Jewish children to come from Europe without visas. The Manchester Guardian reported how Jewish communities and Quakers in the city set up organisations to support refugees. British women – from MP Eleanor Rathbone, to grassroots fundraisers and those who found themselves interned alongside Jews in France – were at the forefront of humanitarian efforts, Winstone said. A 2021 survey by Claims Conference found 21% of the British public knew the UK government was aware of the mass murder of Jews as early as 1941. UK Holocaust Memorial Foundation is co-chaired by the broadcaster and former Labour politician Ed Balls and the Tory peer Eric Pickles, who said the exhibition would give an early insight into the work being developed for the forthcoming memorial. The exhibition will be at the Northern Ireland assembly from 30 October until 13 November; the Scottish parliament from 7 to 10 December; before travelling to Cardiff from 16 January to 4 February 2027, coinciding with Holocaust Memorial Day on 27 January. It is also expected to visit Manchester, with a date and venue yet to be confirmed. The UK Holocaust Memorial and Learning Centre, which would be at Victoria Tower Gardens, Westminster, does not have a confirmed opening date yet, as a planning application is being redetermined by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. The Holocaust Memorial Act 2026 received royal assent this year, granting legal clearance and government funding for the project.

title: Australian tackled, handcuffed by ICE officers in Las Vegas - SMH.com.au
raw_text: An Australian man was left partially handcuffed on the ground by two Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents after they attempted to arrest him in a Las Vegas airport. A video of the incident posted on social media showed the man, in a light blue shirt, screaming “I don’t know what they’re doing” while one of the officers pinned his arm behind his back. One of his shoes had fallen off and his suitcase had been left to the side. The two plainclothes ICE agents – a man and a woman – were both wearing hooded sweatshirts, with the woman also sporting a mask. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said it is making “urgent enquiries” following reports of the arrest. The man who filmed the altercation can be heard asking “what’s going on?” while approaching the two agents. When the male officer realises he’s being recorded, he swipes at the camera. An airport employee then steps between the two and holds his arms out wide, declaring “they’re law enforcement”. Immediately after, the two officers, who have both put their hoods over their heads, walked off and left the distressed man behind, still partially handcuffed. A woman in the video can be seen running after the agents and yelling at them. The incident is reported to have happened on Monday night in Terminal 3 at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas. NBC News reported that the Department of Homeland Security identified the man as 57-year-old Phu Nguyen, an Australian citizen who overstayed his visa. The two agents left without arresting Nguyen “to de-escalate the situation and for officer safety” after a crowd formed, a DHS spokesperson said in a statement to NBC News. ICE arrested him at the Los Angeles International Airport on Tuesday, the Department of Homeland Security told CNN. Nguyen is being held at the Adelanto ICE Processing Centre in California. “The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is making urgent enquiries following reports of an Australian citizen detained in the United States,” a DFAT spokesperson said in a statement. “The Department stands ready to provide consular assistance to any Australian citizen, should it be requested.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world. title: ‘Fake agents’: Migration operators stripped of credentials in crackdown - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Three migration agents have been suspended or stripped of their registrations after allowing unqualified people to use their credentials to provide immigration advice, in a crackdown exposing further misconduct within Australia’s migration industry. The cases include hundreds of visa applications in which registered migration agents allowed unregistered individuals to provide migration assistance using their government-issued identity numbers, commonly known as “front agent” arrangements. The action marks a more aggressive approach by the federal government after years of criticism over the handling of misconduct complaints and a damning Commonwealth auditor-general report that identified a host of failures in supervising the migration agents who facilitate the arrival of vulnerable people into the country. The Office of the Migration Agents Registration Authority (OMARA) cancelled one agent’s registration after finding hundreds of applications lodged through three business ImmiAccounts – the department’s online portal – involved either undeclared immigration assistance or work performed by people who were not registered migration agents. In another case, an agent was suspended after admitting his son, who was not registered, had provided immigration assistance through the business. Investigators also identified allegations that clients had been given falsified departmental correspondence, creating the impression their visa applications had been lodged when they had not. A third agent was suspended after knowingly allowing another business director to lodge visa applications using his registration number until the person became qualified as a migration agent. Assistant Minister for Citizenship Julian Hill said migrants paying for professional advice should be able to trust the person handling their case was properly qualified. He compared the practice to allowing an unqualified person to operate using the registration of a doctor, lawyer or financial planner. “When people pay a migration agent they rightly expect a qualified person will do the work, not an untrained, unregistered fake agent,” Hill said. OMARA, which sits within the Department of Home Affairs, can caution agents, suspend or cancel their registrations and bar former agents from re-registering. Its investigations team can take disciplinary action when agents breach professional obligations or are found not to be fit and proper to provide immigration assistance. Only registered migration agents, Australian legal practitioners or exempt people can legally provide immigration assistance in Australia. In March, the federal government announced migration agents would have to undertake yearly ethics training and regular refreshers on their obligations to continue helping people obtain Australian visas. A 2024 Australian National Audit Office report found Home Affairs’ regulation of migration agents was not effective, with inadequate monitoring and failures to take timely action on complaints. The audit found the department had failed to properly investigate an agent suspected of involvement in sex trafficking after being alerted by Australian Border Force. It also found an automated renewal system had approved agents despite complaints alleging fraudulent behaviour. One complaint took five years to resolve, while allegations involving cash-for-visa arrangements were dismissed over a technicality. The audit’s findings came after then-home affairs minister Clare O’Neil pledged to overhaul the integrity of the migration system following a series of reports in this masthead exposing the way criminals were hijacking visa schemes for their own gain. Migration Institute of Australia chief executive Peter van Vliet said this year that despite more than 4000 registered agents nationwide, only a “very small” number were sanctioned each year. He also warned that negative media narratives were contributing to migration agents becoming “punching bags” in public debate despite their role in helping migrants and businesses comply with Australian law. A spokesman for OMARA said the sanctioned operators damaged the reputation of the broader profession and undermined confidence in migration advice. “While the vast majority of [registered migration agents] act with integrity and professionalism, there is a small cohort who intentionally seek to undermine the migration program for personal gain,” the spokesman said. title: Home Affairs asks DV survivors to prove abuser relationship 'genuine' - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: A federal government safety net for migrant domestic and family violence (DFV) victim-survivors has been criticised as a stressor and barrier. Lawyers and experts say the Department of Home Affairs needs to rethink a process that requires documentary proof a relationship was "genuine" as part of family violence provisions. Minister for Home Affairs Tony Burke says he has taken the "unprecedented" step of cancelling the visas of DFV perpetrators. For women on temporary visas experiencing domestic and family violence (DFV) in Australia, their perpetrators are often also their visa sponsors. Returning to their home countries is usually unthinkable, as many are terrified of being separated from their Australian children, or they know they will face stigma or abuse over the ended relationship. The Department of Home Affairs has family violence provisions under the Migration Act, but the application asks for proof the relationship was "genuine" via documents that usually do not exist. Lawyers and experts say the department has the process backwards, with many applicants "falling down at the first step". Warning: This story includes details of domestic and family violence. For migrant mother Sophia, which is a name she has chosen to protect her identity, the abuse perpetrated by her then-husband and visa sponsor included physical, verbal and sexual abuse. She also survived coercive control and was not permitted to leave the house, learn English or access money. "He kept our passports, controlled all the money, and made all the decisions," Sophia said. "He controlled my communication and isolated me. "He said, 'If you could contact your sister, if you share anything to your sister … I will deport you'." Sophia said she resorted to secretly collecting cans from bins to exchange for 10 cents each so she could buy food for her child. When the relationship ended, she was eventually supported by Settlement Services International to apply for the Home Affairs family violence provisions. Sophia was required to provide proof her relationship was "genuine" through joint bills, bank accounts, leases, mortgages, or even invitations addressed to the couple. She had access to none of those things due to the coercive control. "It was so difficult to explain to immigration," she said. Sophia applied for the provisions in 2023 and is still waiting. 'Pillars of the relationship' Immigration Advice and Rights Centre senior solicitor Kristie Mellor said the department had its process backwards. "They look at what they call the pillars of the relationship, which includes financial aspects of the relationship, the nature of the household, the social aspects of the relationship, and the nature of the couple's commitment to each other," she said. The department's process means it must decide whether the relationship was "genuine" before assessing claims of DFV. Ms Mellor said the sequence was highly problematic with many clients "falling down at the first step". "I imagine that there would be people who choose to remain in relationships because this process is so daunting and that they're worried about the availability of the documents," she said. "You'd usually be looking at joint bank accounts or things to show they've pooled their finances as a couple. [But] where a client's experienced financial abuse, for example, those documents are essentially impossible." She said if the department were to consider DFV evidence first, then due to the nature of the incidents occurring within an intimate partnership, it could then "assume the relationship is genuine". Ms Mellor said the provisions were "really tricky to navigate without legal assistance", and she feared for those who could not get support. "On average, we get 18 new inquiries each week from victim-survivors of family violence. Last year we referred out more than 250 victim-survivors … due to a lack of funding," she said. 'We're sorry, you have to go home' Legal Aid ACT lawyer Jessica Liao said the provisions excluded swathes of temporary visa holders. "You have to hold a very specific subclass of visa before you can even invoke them," she said. Ms Liao said migrants who were secondary applicants to their partner's student visa were among those excluded. "So if the person experiences family violence in that situation, then there's no way to access those protections," she said. "And Canberra's a big student town," her colleague, Legal Aid ACT lawyer Lyn Payne, said. "There are a lot of people here, international students, and we do see, unfortunately, quite a lot of women who are dependent on their husband's student visa. So the husband's here studying, the wife has come, sometimes there's children, and there's family violence. "The migration advice that we give is there's nothing that you can do. We're sorry, you have to go home. "All they can do if they want to leave the violent relationship, is to leave the country." Ms Payne said this was problematic as a partner's student visa had the potential to lead to permanent skills-based visas, which could compel a victim-survivor to stay in an unsafe relationship for immigration security. When Ms Payne was asked whether she believed the omission of some temporary visas from the provisions was an oversight, she disagreed. "I don't think it's an oversight. I think it's completely deliberate. I mean, I think it's wrong," she said. Status unknown Ms Liao said many clients had little knowledge about their immigration status. "We've even seen people who've come from domestic violence, leave relationships with violence and not realise what visa they were holding," she said. "Even people who are permanent residents, not knowing that they were permanent residents and they could actually leave those relationships without the threat of being sent back or needing to report to the Department of Home Affairs." It is those situations, similar to her own, that have prompted Sophia to share this message with new migrants: "Before moving to Australia, please take the time to understand your rights and Australian laws … knowing these things can help you protect yourself," Sophia said. Perpetrators ask friends to lie Professor of Criminology Marie Segrave has researched temporary migration and DFV. She said perpetrators who were aware of the department's "genuine" relationship test were able to derail it by creating "suspicion". "Perpetrators try to ensure that victims aren't on the lease, that they don't have a shared bank account, that they're basically in control of every aspect of their lives," Professor Segrave said. "They also ask all of their friends and anyone in Australia to make sure that they say that the relationship wasn't genuine, that they didn't trust this person. "They can also demand payment for a visa so that they can say, 'No this person basically was paying me to stay in the country'. "But it was, in fact, part of the pattern of coercion that they were trying to get more money from the victim and trying to control the victim through this creation of a debt." Professor Segrave said that as part of the government's national plan to end violence against women and children, "this would be a major area of reform that would be transformative". 'Unprecedented' visa cancellations In a statement, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said he had expanded the number of visa classes that could access assistance for domestic and family violence, "and lowered the barrier to accessing assistance". "In addition, I have taken the unprecedented step of cancelling the visas of multiple people on the basis of credible accusations of domestic violence, including coercive control," he said. "The character test allows the government to cancel the visa of anyone who doesn't meet the standards of our community, and we can use those powers to protect people in our community." In a separate statement, a Department of Home Affairs spokesperson said there were also processes in place to stop known perpetrators from sponsoring further partner visas. "Any future visa applications by a sponsor who has previously been associated with an application granted under the FVPs [family violence provisions] would be appropriately scrutinised by the department," the spokesperson said. "Limitations apply to the number of partner visas an individual can sponsor", the spokesperson said, including a lifetime limit of two.

title: 438 rejections, $55,000 and a years-long-wait: How international talent is turned away - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Dr Maha Selvanathan applied for 438 jobs in Australia before a rural NSW clinic offered her a role as a general practitioner. It took another three years and $55,000 before she was allowed to start working there. As the federal government struggles to find politically palatable ways to reduce the number of overseas arrivals, a parliamentary inquiry into skilled migration has exposed the growing challenges Australia faces in retaining foreign talent in crucial fields such as medicine. Australian Medical Association president Dr Danielle McMullen told the joint standing committee on migration on Friday that some doctors were going homeless while waiting on a complex and lengthy approvals process. She said highly specialised professionals would be poached by other nations with more streamlined systems, and Australia needed to address its duplicated layers of administration and a lack of support for new arrivals. Selvanathan, an AMA member who also appeared before the inquiry, told this masthead she began her job hunt in Adelaide after moving from Malaysia in 2011 to be with her husband. For months, she sat exams, proved her qualifications and demonstrated her English proficiency. Almost two years later, she was granted permanent residency. But she still didn’t have a job, and she had become subject to the 10-year moratorium, which requires migrant doctors to work in areas of high need for a decade. “I got rejection after rejection, and I got one offer from Armidale,” she says. Then there were more exams, and the regulator had to give its approval. Plus, the one clinic that had offered her a job was not already classified as being in need. For six months, the clinic advertised for a doctor to prove it could not get one. Selvanathan waited, barred from working in her field. She uprooted and moved to Sydney, ready to relocate again to Armidale. Her husband followed her there, but he could not get a job in the city of less than 24,000 people for almost eight months because he worked in IT. Throughout the process, she squirrelled away funds to return to Malaysia so she could keep her clinical skills up to date. “It was very depressing because I don’t know what my future holds,” she said. “There was always this praying and waiting whether this will go through, ‘will my registration go through, will my supervision go through’. So it was just very upsetting and a lot of money.” McMullen said more than half of Australia’s GPs were international medical graduates, who prop up rural medical services. They should be celebrated rather than being treated as a “temporary fix for poor workforce planning”, she said. She pointed to a lack of rural housing as a significant barrier. Logistical challenges were compounded by a “deep-set culture” of racism that meant migrant doctors were often forced out of roles, or lived in fear of speaking up against discrimination because their visa was tied to their employer, she said. “It is deeply concerning that we’ve got doctors essentially living in even short periods of homelessness. It is not, I think, what the community would expect,” she said. Liberal MP Leon Rebello, the migration committee’s deputy chair, said the housing challenge was a recurring theme across Friday’s testimony from numerous industries, from law to medicine and science. “That nexus between housing and immigration is going to be critical going forward,” Rebello said. “You can’t set migration numbers without giving due consideration to the infrastructure and the housing that Australia could take, and that’s ultimately the key.” As Prime Minister Anthony Albanese scrambles to get the Coalition onside for laws that will help the government hit a forecast 225,000 net migration target in two years time, Labor premiers have split. NSW Premier Chris Minns said governments needed to stop relying on migration to boost productivity and South Australia’s Peter Malinauskas has framed sweeping cuts as economic self-harm. Asked about Malinauskas’ comments on Friday, Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said immigration was crucial to the economy and should not be “kicked around like a political football”. But in echoes of the opposition, which has vowed to limit annual migration to the number of homes built per year, Marles said: “That said, immigration needs to be pegged at a level which matches our infrastructure, our services.” Selvanathan did not want to weigh in on the broader political debate but she said she did know Australia needed to retain more doctors. She said many of her friends had given up on a career in medicine and had retrained in other professions, such as banking. “Complete wasted skills,” she said.
